etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English spillen, from Old English spillan, spildan (“to kill, destroy, waste”), from Proto-West Germanic *spilþijan, from Proto-Germanic *spilþijaną (“to spoil, kill, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to sunder, split, rend, tear”).

Cognate with Dutch spillen (“to use needlessly, waste”), French gaspiller ("to waste, squander" < Germanic), Bavarian spillen (“to split, cleave, splinter”), Danish spilde (“to spill, waste”), Swedish spilla (“to spill, waste”), Icelandic spilla (“to contaminate, spoil”). See also spool.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To drop something so that it spreads out or makes a mess; to accidentally pour.
(intransitive) To spread out or fall out, as above.

quote.citation: 1741, I[saac] Watts, The Improvement of the Mind: Or, A Supplement to the Art of Logick: […], London:  […]  James Brackstone, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He was so topful of himself, that he let it spill on all the company.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of a crowd or people within a crowd) To overflow out of a designated area.
(transitive) To drop something that was intended to be caught.

quote.citation: 2011 October 29, Neil Johnston, “Norwich 3 - 3 Blackburn”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: That should have been that, but Hart caught a dose of the Hennessey wobbles and spilled Adlene Guedioura's long-range shot.

definitions.definition: To mar; to damage; to destroy by misuse; to waste.

quote.citation: 1589, George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie:
quote.text: They [the colours] disfigure the stuff and spill the whole workmanship.

quote.citation: 1642, Thomas Fuller, The Holy State, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire:  […]  Roger Daniel for John Williams, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Spill not the morning (the quintessence of day) in recreations.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To be destroyed, ruined, or wasted; to come to ruin; to perish; to waste.

quote.citation: 1387–1400, Geoffrey Chaucer, “The Man of Lawes Tale”, in The Canterbury Tales, [Westminster: William Caxton, published 1478], →OCLC; republished in [William Thynne], editor, The Workes of Geffray Chaucer Newlye Printed, […], [London]:  […]  [Richard Grafton for] Iohn Reynes […], 1542, →OCLC:
quote.text: That thou wilt suffer innocence to spill.(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: 16th century, Anonymous, "The Old Cloak", st. 1, as reported in The Oxford Book of English Verse (1900):
quote.text: This winter’s weather it waxeth cold, / And frost it freezeth on every hill, / And Boreas blows his blast so bold / That all our cattle are like to spill.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To overflow or flow out, over or off something.
(transitive) To cause or flow out and be lost or wasted; to shed.

quote.citation: 1665 (first performance), John Dryden, The Indian Emperour, or, The Conquest of Mexico by the Spaniards. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for H[enry] Herringman […], published 1667, →OCLC, Act IV, scene ii, page 44:
quote.text: to revenge his Blood, ſo juſtly ſpilt, / VVhat is it leſs then to partake his guilt?

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang, obsolete) To cause to be thrown from a mount, a carriage, etc.

quote.citation: 2007, Eric Flint, David Weber, 1634: The Baltic War:
quote.text: Then, not thirty feet beyond, a sudden panicky lunge to the side by his horse spilled him from the saddle.

definitions.definition: To cover or decorate with slender pieces of wood, metal, ivory, etc.; to inlay.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto X”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: And all the others pavement were with yvory spilt

definitions.definition: (nautical) To relieve a sail from the pressure of the wind, so that it can be more easily reefed or furled, or to lessen the strain.
(transitive, Australian politics) To open the leadership of a parliamentary party for re-election.
(transitive, intransitive) To reveal information to an uninformed party.

quote.citation: 1932, Delos W. Lovelace, King Kong, published 1965, page 32:
quote.text: ‘You wanted to know where we were going. Follow me. I’m going to spill it.’

definitions.definition: (of a knot) To come undone.
(transitive) To express (something), especially repeatedly or floridly; to be expressed.
(countable) A mess of something that has been dropped.
A fall or stumble.
A small stick or piece of paper used to light a candle, cigarette etc by the transfer of a flame from a fire.

quote.citation: 2008, Elizabeth Bear, Ink and Steel: A Novel of the Promethean Age:
quote.text: Kit froze with the pipe between his teeth, the relit spill pressed to the weed within it.

definitions.definition: A peg or pin for plugging a hole, as in a cask; a spile.
A metallic rod or pin.
A spillikin.

quote.citation: 1971, Gwen White, Antique Toys And Their Background, page 125:
quote.text: A tool with which to extract the spills from the pile.

definitions.definition: (Shropshire, Herefordshire) A splinter caught in the skin.
A slender piece of anything.
(mining) One of the thick laths or poles driven horizontally ahead of the main timbering in advancing a level in loose ground.
(sound recording) The situation where sound is picked up by a microphone from a source other than that which is intended.
(obsolete) A small sum of money.

quote.citation: 1726, John Ayliffe, Parergon Juris Canonici Anglicani: Or, A Commentary, by Way of Supplement to the Canons and Constitutions of the Church of England. […], London:  […]  D. Leach, and sold by John Walthoe […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Spill or Sportule for the same from the credulous Laity

definitions.definition: (Australian politics) A declaration that the leadership of a parliamentary party is vacant, and open for re-election. Short form of leadership spill.

pronunciation: l-vocalizing: UK, General Australian, New Zealand
